meetings.title: Durham City Council May 15, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: Celebrating former Durham mayors with St. Joseph's and Watts Street Boy Scouts, the council proclaimed Robert Wense Grabarek's 98th birthday and National Gun Violence Awareness Day before unanimously passing all formal votes (7-0), including the consent agenda (with Item 14 Fayette Place purchase and Item 17 Heritage Park/GoDurham ADA items pulled for brief discussion), two West Club Boulevard historic landmark ordinances, and annexation/rezoning for 815 East Geer Street. No split votes occurred on May 15, though Council held extended debate on Item 30—a proposed resolution rescinding six previously ordered 2007-era county utility extension petitions whose estimated city/petitioner costs had surged by roughly $1.7M-$2.15M due to NCDOT shoring rules and elapsed time—voting unanimously to keep the hearing open until June 19 while seeking NCDOT relief and NC Utilities Commission input on the failing Grand Oaks/Red Coach package sewer plant.

agenda_items.title: Former Mayors Reunion, Robert Wense Grabarek Day, and National Gun Violence Awareness Day
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Eddie Davis led a salute to former living Durham mayors (including Sylvia Kerchoff, Nick Tennyson, and Bill/Mary Ann Bell guests) and read a proclamation declaring May 21, 2017 as Robert Wense Grabarek Day honoring the former mayor's 1963 civil rights interim committee leadership at age 98. Mayor Bell also proclaimed June 2, 2017 as National Gun Violence Awareness Day ('Wear Orange').

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 14, 17, and General Business Items)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council pulled Item 14 (Fayette Place) and Item 17 (police/fleet/GoDurham or Heritage Park items) for citizen/council discussion and approved the remainder of the consent agenda unanimously.

agenda_items.title: FY 2017-2018 Budget Presentation (Manager Tom Bonfield) & Pulled Consent Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented his proposed FY 2017-2018 budget featuring a 4% average merit pay pool (5% public safety), a $15/hr minimum city wage, 12 weeks paid parental leave, and an initial plan toward doubling the dedicated housing fund. Council also unanimously cleared the pulled consent items after questions on GoDurham/Heritage Park contract terms and Fayette Place financing.

agenda_items.title: Local Historic Landmark Designation (1058 W. Club Blvd) & Annexation/Rezoning (815 E. Geer St)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously designated 1058 West Club Boulevard as a local historic landmark following a brief property-tax/preservation question from Charlie Reece, and unanimously approved voluntary annexation, utility extension, consistency statement, and residential rezoning for 815 East Geer Street in sequential unanimous votes concluding at 01:43:08.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Rescission of Six Previously Ordered Petitioned Utility Improvements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works Engineering Manager Robert Joyner outlined steep cost increases (~$1.74M-$2.15M+) caused by new NCDOT asphalt reconstruction and steel shoring mandates on six county utility extensions ordered in 2007-2010 (including failing septic systems and the Grand Oaks/Red Coach package treatment plant). After affected county homeowners urged the city not to rescind 10-year promises and Council Members Don Moffitt, Steve Schewel, and Charlie Reece debated city-taxpayer equity vs. moral obligations, council continued the public hearing to June 19.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Unpulled Items)
votes.notes: Voice vote unanimous at 00:45:38.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved routine consent items excluding pulled Items 14 and 17.

votes.item_title: Pulled Consent Items (Fayette Place / Housing / Transit Items)
votes.notes: Unanimous voice approval at 01:14:23.
votes.discussion_detail: Clears pulled consent items after manager budget presentation and staff clarifications.

votes.item_title: 1058 West Club Boulevard Historic Landmark Designation Ordinance
votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote across two actions at 01:34:29 and 01:35:55.
votes.discussion_detail: Designates 1058 W. Club Blvd as local historic landmark.

votes.item_title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning — 815 East Geer Street
votes.notes: Unanimous voice approvals at 01:37:08 and 01:43:08.
votes.discussion_detail: Approves annexation and residential rezoning on East Geer Street.

votes.item_title: Item 30: Continue Public Hearing on Rescission of Six Utility Petitions to June 19
votes.notes: Continuance passed unanimously at 02:45:01; adjournment followed at 02:47:13.
votes.discussion_detail: Continues Item 30 to allow work-session analysis of NCDOT costs, unit counts, and package-plant legal posture.

disagreements.issue: City Obligation vs. County Cost Subsidy on Six Petitioned Utility Extensions (Item 30)
disagreements.summary: Although council voted unanimously to continue the hearing to June 19 for additional data, members differed over whether Durham city taxpayers should absorb ~$2 million in NCDOT-driven utility cost overruns for non-city subdivisions ordered in 2007.
disagreements.side_a_position: Avoid rescinding 2007 city commitments made to homeowners who have waited ten years on failing septic/well or package-sewer systems.
side_a_arguments: Petitioners voted on city assessments a decade ago and planned their lives around promised utility extensions; sudden rescission penalizes them for state DOT changes and municipal delays.
disagreements.side_b_position: Verify county responsibility, package-plant owner obligations, and per-homeowner subsidy figures before spending up to $2 million in city utility/general funds outside city limits.
side_b_arguments: Other failed-subdivision homeowners in the county do not automatically pay city taxes unless annexed, and state utility/transportation agencies share responsibility for Grand Oaks and NCDOT shoring costs.
disagreements.resolution: Continued unanimously (7-0) at 02:45:01 for work-session analysis and June 19 continuation.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presided over the May 4, 2017 City Council Work Session, opening with unanimous approval of the City Manager's priority items (including supplemental Item 25 designating John Hope Franklin Memorial Highway). During consent review, Council Member Steve Schewel questioned Planning staff on the FY 2018 Planning Work Program regarding tree conservation and mass grading text amendments, Transportation staff on 100 traffic congestion CCTV cameras and pedestrian countdown timers, and staff on a reentry workforce grant contract with Eckerd. Council received two major presentations: the Durham Bike+Walk Implementation Plan outlining 75 prioritized pedestrian, bicycle, intersection, and sidewalk projects, and the proposed FY 2017-18 Water and Sewer Rates maintaining one cent per tier for watershed protection while projecting modest tier increases and lower five-year rate trajectories due to strong revenue growth. Council closed by unanimously setting the upcoming regular meeting agenda, granting an excused absence for July 20, and voting unanimously to enter closed session.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Priority Items, and Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the session to order and Council unanimously approved the Manager's priority items scheduling presentations on Items 6 and 7, adding supplemental Item 25 (John Hope Franklin Memorial Highway designation), and noting a post-meeting closed session under GS 143-318.11(a)(5). Council pulled Items 3, 5, 8, 10, and 14, heard citizen speaker John Tarantino, and skipped previewing Item 18 (FY 2017-18 budget presentation scheduled for May 15).
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed (Unanimous voice vote on priority items)

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Items: Planning Work Program, Signal System, Insurance, and Reentry Grant
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On Item 3 (FY18 Planning Work Program), Planning staff (Scott Whiteman) told Council Member Steve Schewel that tree coverage, mass grading, and buffering text amendments were grouped under Section 4.1.2 and noted Planning Commissioner Whitley's lone no vote stemmed from wanting a broad East Durham planning initiative. Council also questioned Item 5 (100 congestion CCTV cameras and retrofitting pedestrian countdown timers), Item 8 ($3M property/casualty insurance coverage aligned with peer NC cities), and Item 10 (scoring criteria for the Eckerd workforce reentry contract).

agenda_items.title: Item 6: Durham Bike+Walk Implementation Plan Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation staff presented the Stantec-assisted Durham Bike+Walk Implementation Plan, detailing a data-driven and equity-weighted process narrowing needs to 75 projects (17 pedestrian focus, 8 bike focus, 25 intersections, and 25 sidewalk gaps). Council members requested a breakdown of projects on state versus local roads, asked how the 75 projects compare against existing 10-year CIP funding, and inquired about wide/protected bike lane designs.

agenda_items.title: Item 7: Proposed FY 2017-18 Water and Sewer Rates Presentation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Management presented proposed FY 2017-18 rate adjustments across tiers (raising a Tier 1 bill from $21.04 to $21.64/month and an average Tier 3 bill from $56.18 to $57.64) while continuing one penny per tier for watershed protection. Staff highlighted that higher water consumption and project savings allowed lower five-year projected increases and pushed out revenue bond borrowing, though long-term rates still depend on Jordan Lake rules.

agenda_items.title: Agenda Setting, Excused Absence, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously set the upcoming City Council meeting agenda (Consent 1-17 and 25; GBA 18; GBA public hearings 19-23), unanimously approved an excused absence request for the July 20 work session, and voted unanimously to enter closed session.

votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved priority scheduling for Items 6 and 7, supplemental Item 25 (John Hope Franklin Memorial Highway), and post-meeting closed session.

votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved Consent items 1-17 and 25, GBA item 18, and GBA public hearing items 19-23.

votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote; requester's name was not spoken in the transcript.
votes.discussion_detail: Approved a council member's excused absence request for the July 20 work session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council May 1, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: On International Workers' Day, public speakers addressed unpaid jail labor before the council honored the MEAC champion NCCU men's basketball team and Coach LeVelle Moton and heard Durham County/DPD leadership. All formal votes passed unanimously (7-0), including the consent agenda—which funded purchase of the vacant Fayette Place site despite sharp criticism from Council Members Charlie Reece and Steve Schewel over last-minute process and lack of a costed redevelopment plan—an NC 55 sidewalk reimbursement agreement (7-0), and the consolidated annexation and rezoning of 3130 Hursey Street for up to 179 townhomes (7-0). Following the votes, Police Chief C.J. Davis delivered the First Quarter 2017 Crime Report, sparking substantial policy questioning from Council Members Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, and Eddie Davis regarding written consent-search forms, police checkpoints, and rising gun violence.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment on Jail Labor & Proclamation for NCCU Men's Basketball Championship
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following opening prayer and public testimony from an advocate reading a letter by a formerly incarcerated worker regarding unpaid kitchen/janitorial labor at the Durham County Jail, Mayor Bell and Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden presented a proclamation honoring NCCU Coach LeVelle Moton and the men's basketball team for winning the 2017 MEAC Championship and reaching the NCAA Tournament.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Including Fayette Place Property Acquisition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda 7-0, including an agreement to acquire the former Fayette Place public housing site. Immediately following the consent vote, Charlie Reece and Steve Schewel criticized adding the acquisition to consent without a prior work-session vetting, development budget, or master-plan clarity, while Eddie Davis and Mayor Bell argued securing the land in public hands preserved affordable housing flexibility.

agenda_items.title: Utility/Sidewalk Reimbursement Agreement Along NC 55
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation and public works staff presented a reimbursement agreement coordinating sidewalk improvements along NC Highway 55 to avoid duplicating construction costs. Council approved the item unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning: 3130 Hursey Street (179 Townhomes)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a voluntary annexation and zoning map change for 3130 Hursey Street allowing up to 179 townhomes with connectivity and road improvements reviewed against prior neighbor access concerns. Council approved the annexation, consistency statement, and rezoning unanimously across sequential votes.

agenda_items.title: Durham Police Department First Quarter 2017 Crime Report (Chief C.J. Davis)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chief C.J. Davis reported first-quarter Part I crime trends, highlighting shootings, homicides, robbery enforcement, and self-defense UCR classifications. Council Members Jillian Johnson and Charlie Reece challenged the decline in written consent-search documentation since adopting written forms and questioned traffic-checkpoint practices, while Eddie Davis raised neighborhood gun-violence prevention.

votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote at 00:52:11.
votes.discussion_detail: Coordinates sidewalk construction funding along NC 55.

votes.item_title: Item 24: Consolidated Annexation & Rezoning — 3130 Hursey Street
votes.notes: Two sequential unanimous voice votes at 01:21:23 and 01:21:30.
votes.discussion_detail: Approves residential annexation and zoning for 3130 Hursey Street.

disagreements.issue: Process & Financial Clarity Around Fayette Place Purchase (Consent Item)
disagreements.summary: Although council voted 7-0 on the consent agenda approving the Fayette Place purchase, members sharply disagreed on placing a multimillion-dollar land purchase directly onto consent without work-session vetting or redevelopment cost estimates.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support buying Fayette Place immediately to bring the land under public control for future affordable housing.
side_a_arguments: Securing the parcel before private developers acquire it preserves long-term affordable housing leverage near downtown.
disagreements.side_b_position: Support the goal of acquiring Fayette Place but object to bypassing work-session review and lacking clear master-plan and subsidy numbers before voting.
side_b_arguments: Placing major acquisitions directly on consent deprives residents and council of public vetting on full lifecycle costs and opportunity costs.
disagreements.resolution: Approved 7-0 on the consent agenda at 00:43:16; remarks entered for future process accountability.

disagreements.issue: DPD Written Consent-Search Policy, Probable Cause & Checkpoints (Q1 Crime Report)
disagreements.summary: During the non-voting Q1 crime briefing, council members questioned Chief C.J. Davis over enforcement disparities, declining documented consent searches alongside persistent warrantless searches, and checkpoint deployment.
disagreements.side_a_position: Scrutinize whether police officers are shifting from written consent searches to undocumented probable-cause searches and whether checkpoints strain community trust.
side_a_arguments: Following council's written consent-search mandate, overall search transparency must not evaporate into discretionary stop-and-search exceptions or unmonitored neighborhood checkpoints.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defend officer adherence to written consent forms while preserving tactical flexibility for traffic enforcement and hot-spot crime abatement.
side_b_arguments: Checkpoints and targeted operations respond to specific neighborhood safety requests and violent crime patterns while following departmental general orders.
disagreements.resolution: Informational report concluded without a formal vote.

meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presided over the April 20, 2017 City Council Work Session, opening with unanimous votes to approve the City Manager's priority item (a presentation on Item 20, the Upper Neuse River Basin Association budget) and a brief City Clerk item. During agenda review, members praised Kimley-Horn's UBE participation on Item 5 (water main and metering work) and pulled Items 16 and 17, followed by a citizen matter regarding parking, trash, and open-container concerns on an unimproved city street near Drew Street where Police Lt. Vaughn explained legal enforcement limits. In the second half, staff briefed Council on the UNRBA's $1,025,600 FY 2017-18 budget—its first above $1 million—and efforts to lobby the General Assembly to extend Falls Lake Stage 2 rule deadlines from 2021 to 2023, as well as the Urban Open Space Plan ahead of its May 15 public hearing. agenda_items.title: Citizen Matters: Unimproved City Street Access and WomenNC

Police District 1 Commander Lt. Vaughn and legal staff explained that legal street parking cannot be prohibited and noted they were reviewing open-container enforceability between public right-of-way and private property, while also discussing statutory street-vacation options before WomenNC Advocacy Chair Jamie Cole began addressing Item 27.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Apr 17, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: Opening with Neighborhood Spotlight honors for Alice Cheek, Steve McNulty, and Rob Cornes, the Durham City Council passed every item on its agenda unanimously (7-0) by show of hands because the electronic voting machine was offline. Key approvals included the consent agenda (7-0), rezoning cases at 404/406 N. Driver Street (7-0), 2013 & 2015 N. Miami Boulevard (7-0), and 6103/6107 Farrington Road (7-0), plus Fendol Farms Phase II (Item 14, 7-0) after council debated whether the developer could be pressed via a 30-day deferral to preserve an 1849 farmhouse before concluding prior development approvals left no legal leverage. Council also approved conduit tax-exempt multifamily bonds for Southview Apartments (7-0) after pressing Reinvestment Partners/developer teams on minority business participation, and approved annual evaluations for City Manager Tom Bonfield and City Attorney Patrick Baker (7-0).

agenda_items.title: Neighborhood Spotlight Awards & Consent Agenda Approval
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell noted the voting machine was inoperable, requiring show-of-hands voting, and presented Neighborhood Spotlight Awards to Alice Cheek (Edgemont Elms) and Steve McNulty and Rob Cornes (Milan Woods). Council then approved the consent agenda unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Rezoning & Annexation Cases: 404/406 N. Driver St, 2013/2015 N. Miami Blvd & 6103/6107 Farrington Rd
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council conducted public hearings and unanimously approved three development requests: a zoning map change at 404/406 North Driver Street (00:40:13), a commercial/office rezoning at 2013 and 2015 North Miami Boulevard (00:45:39), and a consolidated annexation and rezoning at 6103 and 6107 Farrington Road (00:55:22).

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change & Plan Amendment: Fendol Farms (1849 Farmhouse Preservation Debate)

Council Member Steve Schewel asked whether a 30-day deferral could incentivize a compromise, but Charlie Reece and city attorneys advised council lacked authority under state law after earlier site approvals, resulting in unanimous approval.

disagreements.issue: Historic Farmhouse Preservation vs. Prior Zoning Vesting: Fendol Farms (Item 14)
disagreements.summary: Following testimony from local preservationists seeking to save an 1849 farmhouse on the Fendol Farms tract, Council Member Steve Schewel explored a 30-day deferral while colleagues noted statutory and vested-rights limits before voting unanimously 7-0.
disagreements.side_a_position: Explore a 30-day deferral to encourage the developer and preservationists to negotiate saving or relocating the 1849 farmhouse.
side_a_arguments: A brief pause might prompt creative private preservation solutions before demolition proceeds.
disagreements.side_b_position: Proceed to a vote because prior approved development entitlements left council with only an up-or-down zoning choice without legal authority to compel preservation.
side_b_arguments: Years had passed since initial approval and state law forbids conditioning rezonings on historic preservation beyond voluntary proffers.
disagreements.resolution: Council opted against deferring and passed Item 14 unanimously 7-0 at 01:30:16.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presided over the April 6, 2017 City Council Work Session with all seven council members present. Council unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items (pulling Item 7 on watershed protection for a presentation) and the City Attorney's priority item for a closed session on Adrian Block v. City of Durham. Staff presented on the watershed protection land-acquisition prioritization model funded by the one-cent-per-CCF water fee (~$100,000/year) and on Public Works' stormwater control measure (SCM) inspection program, highlighting 100% annual third-party reviews, 20% city QA inspections, and a remediation case study at Renaissance at Southpoint. Council also held a lengthy briefing and discussion on the $2.476 billion Durham-Orange Light Rail Transit (LRT) plan—examining the 30% contingency, $1.82 billion total local capital and financing cost through 2062, sales-tax growth assumptions, and concerns over potential bus-service trade-offs, with Mayor Bell noting Council's indirect vote via MPO and GoTriangle seats—before reporting Planning Commission ballot tallies, unanimously setting the regular meeting agenda, and entering closed session.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Announcements, Priority Items, and Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the session to order with all seven council members present. Following an announcement promoting the Full Frame Documentary Film Festival, Council unanimously approved the Manager's priority items (pulling Item 7 and noting Scott Bart would not appear) and the Attorney's priority item for a closed session on Adrian Block v. City of Durham, then reviewed consent, presentation, and public hearing items.

agenda_items.title: Item 7: Watershed Protection Prioritization and Conservation Trust Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Water Management staff presented a GIS-based prioritization framework—adapted from Raleigh's Upper Neuse Clean Water Initiative with Triangle Land Conservancy—to guide watershed protection purchases and easements using the ~$100,000/year generated by the one-cent-per-CCF fee authorized in 2011. Council confirmed outreach could partner with any qualifying land trust active in Durham's watersheds.

agenda_items.title: Item 12: Stormwater Control Measures (SCMs) and Maintenance Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public Works staff (Shea Bullock) outlined Durham's SCM inventory (dry/wet detention basins and underground sand filters), commercial maintenance guarantees, and inspection regime requiring annual third-party inspections on 100% of devices with 20% receiving onsite city QA checks. Staff walked through a multi-year remediation timeline at Renaissance at Southpoint Phase 1 stormwater wetland.

agenda_items.title: Item 11: Durham County Transit Plan and Light Rail Transit (LRT) Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: GoTriangle and transit staff detailed the $2.476 billion LRT capital budget (including a 30% contingency exceeding FTA's 25% expectation), the 82/18 county split, total capital and financing costs of $1.82 billion through 2062 TIFFIA repayment, 2020 federal grant milestones, and 4.33% sales-tax growth assumptions ahead of late-April county, MPO, and GoTriangle board votes. One council member voiced concern over historical transit cost overruns, commuter rail realism, and risks to bus service, while Mayor Bell and other members underscored staying the course and noted Council's indirect leverage through its MPO and GoTriangle representatives.

agenda_items.title: Planning Commission Ballot, Agenda Setting, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council recorded Planning Commission votes (DeRiana Freeman 7 votes; Cynthia Satterfield 4 votes), unanimously set the next regular City Council meeting agenda (Consent 1-10 and GBA public hearings 13-18), and voted unanimously to enter closed session.

votes.notes: Unanimous voice vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Apr 3, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: In a brief 31-minute session, Mayor Bill Bell and the Durham City Council issued four civic proclamations recognizing Sjogren's Syndrome Awareness Month, Sexual Assault Awareness Month (with the Durham Crisis Response Center), the graduates of Durham's first Citizen Water Academy, and Animal Services Appreciation Week. Council then unanimously approved the consent agenda (7-0)—including reappointing a member to the Passenger Vehicle for Hire Commission (Item 5)—and voted 7-0 on Item 21 to open the mandatory 30-day public comment period on the draft FY 2017-2018 Annual Action Plan for federal HUD housing grants (May 19 through June 19, 2017). All actions were routine and unanimous, with no split votes or substantive policy disagreements.

agenda_items.title: Civic Proclamations (Sjogren's Awareness, Sexual Assault Awareness, Citizen Water Academy & Animal Services)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell and Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden presented proclamations for Sjogren's Syndrome Awareness Month and Sexual Assault Awareness Month with Durham Crisis Response Center representatives. Water Management staff recognized graduates of the first Citizen Water Academy, and council also proclaimed National Animal Care and Control Appreciation Week honoring Durham County Animal Services.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda & Passenger Vehicle for Hire Commission Reappointment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read consent items 1-20, noting Items 21 and 22 were on the general business agenda and highlighting Item 5's mayoral nominee for reappointment to the Passenger Vehicle for Hire Commission. meetings.title: Durham City Council Mar 20, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council celebrated the 43rd Annual Durham CROP Hunger Walk (now second largest in the nation), proclaimed Pauli Murray Family Home National Historic Landmark Day, and congratulated Morehead Montessori's chess team before approving every legislative item 7-0. Council appointed David Folloroff to the Recreation Advisory Commission (4 ballot votes), unanimously approved three AT&T/Teleport/BellSouth fiber-installation right-of-way license renewals (7-0) only after Steve Schewel, Charlie Reece, and Don Moffitt sharply questioned Public Works and AT&T officials over utility line hits, 44+ stop-work incidents, and state preemption of local right-of-way fees. Council also voted 7-0 to send UDO Traffic Impact Analysis expiration amendment TC16-00002 back to staff for Planning Commission re-review after developer legal challenges, closed 180 feet of Shawnee Street for a greenway easement (7-0), and approved annexations/zonings for Mount Level Missionary Baptist Church (7-0) and Shiloh Glen I & II (7-0).

Steve Schewel presented a proclamation declaring April 1, 2017 Pauli Murray Family Home National Historic Landmark Day, and Charlie Reece congratulated Morehead Montessori's chess team and Council Member Jillian Johnson's son Elias on placing at the state championships.

agenda_items.title: Teleport Communications / AT&T Corp. / BellSouth Telecom Right-of-Way License Renewals

Steve Schewel, Charlie Reece, and Don Moffitt criticized North Carolina legislation stripping municipal right-of-way user fees while leaving city inspectors uncompensated; council nevertheless passed all three license agreements 7-0.

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment TC16-00002: Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) Expiration Standards

disagreements.issue: Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) Expiration vs. Master-Plan Vesting Rights (Item 26)
disagreements.summary: Developer attorneys and Planning Commission opponents argued expiring approved TIAs after two to four years unlawfully modifies vested master-plan zonings (such as Bethpage and Davis Park), prompting Don Moffitt and fellow council members to pause and refer staff's revised UDO text back to the Planning Commission.
disagreements.side_a_position: Require updated TIAs and updated mitigation when large master-planned projects stall for many years so current traffic conditions are reflected.
side_a_arguments: Applying uniform TIA expiration rules prevents decade-old traffic assumptions from locking in outdated infrastructure commitments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Return the heavily revised staff text to the Planning Commission rather than risking unlawful alteration of committed development plans.
side_b_arguments: Planning Commission previously denied the earlier draft 5-7 on legal vesting concerns and had not reviewed staff's subsequent edits.
disagreements.resolution: Referred back to staff and Planning Commission 7-0 at 01:40:36.

meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presided over the March 9, 2017 City Council Work Session with all members present except Don Moffitt (excused absence). meetings.title: Durham City Council March 6, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: Opening with Mayor Bill Bell's rebuttal letter to Senate Leader Phil Berger opposing claims about Durham in state Senate Bill 145, the council approved an excused absence, the city manager's priority referral of Farrington Road water fees (7-0), and the consent agenda (7-0) before receiving Chief C.J. Davis's 2016 Annual Crime Report (showing a 4% overall drop in Part I crime and 20-year low in burglaries alongside a 17% uptick in robberies and 42 homicides). On Item 17, council split and defeated 3-4 a staff-recommended stormwater ordinance amendment modifying Jordan Lake nutrient/buffer rules to align with state legislation (the electronic tally failed 3-4 without the clerk reading all seven individual votes aloud; Charlie Reece explicitly stated he would vote No to defend Durham's active federal permit through February 2018 rather than pre-emptively weakening Jordan Lake protections, while Steve Schewel, Cora Cole-McFadden, and Don Moffitt favored working with DEQ on compliance). Council concluded with a public hearing on the FY 2017-2018 budget and CIP (accepted 7-0), where advocates pushed for a $15/hour living wage for city contractors and a major affordable housing bond.

agenda_items.title: Mayor's SB 145 Letter, Excused Absence, Farrington Road Referral & Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council unanimously approved a member's excused absences, approved City Manager Tom Bonfield's priority referral of Item 5 (Farrington Road water line fees) back to administration, and passed the consent agenda 7-0. Mayor Bell also read a letter sent to Senator Phil Berger correcting state Senate Bill 145's assertions regarding Durham's compliance with federal and state law.

agenda_items.title: 2016 Annual Crime Report Presentation (Police Chief C.J. Davis)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief C.J. Davis presented 2016 crime metrics: overall Part I crime declined 4% (burglaries fell 19% to a 20-year low, aggravated assaults fell 6%, larcenies -1%), while violent crime rose 2% driven by a 17% jump in robberies (68% with firearms) and 42 homicides. She detailed staffing (89% sworn filled / 59 vacancies), take-home patrol cars for city residents, body-worn cameras rolling out to Districts 1 and 4, and new de-escalation and simulator training.

agenda_items.title: Stormwater Permit Modifications & Jordan Lake Rules Ordinance Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Stormwater and City Attorney staff presented ordinance amendments stripping Jordan Lake state nutrient/buffer language to resolve a legal conflict created after the General Assembly placed Jordan Lake rules in abeyance while seeking DEQ permit clarity. Don Moffitt, Steve Schewel, and Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden supported engaging DEQ on compliant permit text, Mayor Bell pressed staff on detention-pond enforcement liens, and Charlie Reece opposed dropping protections while Durham held a valid federal permit through February 2018; the motion failed 3-4.

agenda_items.title: First Public Hearing: FY 2017-2018 Budget & FY 2018-2023 Capital Improvement Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Budget Director Bertha Johnson opened the first budget and CIP public hearing. Residents, Durham Can/labor advocates, and affordable-housing speakers urged extending the $15/hour living wage to contracted workers, increasing dedicated funding/bonds for affordable housing to meet 2016 housing goals, funding sidewalks, and maintaining public safety accountability; council voted 7-0 to accept comments for the record and adjourned at 9:12 p.m.

disagreements.issue: Retaining Jordan Lake Stormwater Protections vs. State Statutory Compliance (Item 17)
disagreements.summary: Council defeated 3-4 a staff recommendation to remove Jordan Lake stormwater ordinance language and seek DEQ permit modifications after state legislation placed Jordan Lake rules in abeyance (only Charlie Reece explicitly declared a No vote on the mic during final debate before the un-read 3-4 electronic tally; Steve Schewel, Cora Cole-McFadden, and Don Moffitt expressed support for working with DEQ).

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the February 23, 2017 City Council Work Session presided over by Mayor Bill Bell, the Council approved the City Manager's priority items—including an announcement of Kavala, Greece as Durham's newest Sister City—and unanimously set the upcoming regular meeting agenda by voice vote. During Citizens Matters, speakers addressed record-expungement and Second Chance Lobby Day advocacy backed by Emerald City, and CeaseFire Durham representative Mark Simmons presented policing reform recommendations focused on relationship-based policing, de-escalation, and officer training incentives, prompting a staff update on DPD's evaluation of PERF's ICAT training and potential DOJ COPS grant funding. Council Member Charlie Reece introduced a resolution opposing the January 27, 2017 presidential executive order on immigration and refugee resettlement and proclaiming May 6, 2017 as Durham Refugees Day, though the middle portion of the transcript covering any immediate floor action is omitted. Council also questioned staff and legal counsel on proposed Jordan Lake stormwater permit and ordinance revisions—weighing developer litigation risk against maintaining stricter stormwater standards through the February 2018 NPDES permit renewal—as well as the FY 2016-2017 Second Quarter Financial Report projecting a >$7 million positive General Fund variance and an HR agreement with The Mercer Group to modernize employee performance evaluations.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Agenda Deferral Request, and Priority Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the February 23, 2017 work session to order, and the City Clerk called the roll with Eddie Davis noted as on his way and Bill Bell, Cora Cole-McFadden, Jillian Johnson, Don Moffitt, Charlie Reece, and Steve Schewel present. Charlie Reece requested deferring his added resolution (Item 21) until after Citizens Matters. The Deputy City Manager presented a priority item regarding Sister Cities of Durham announcing Kavala, Greece as a new sister city with a short presentation, which Council approved by voice vote; the City Attorney and City Clerk had no priority items.

agenda_items.title: Review of Draft Regular Agenda Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff and Council reviewed upcoming agenda items and flagged items to pull for work session discussion, including an NCDOT last-mile agreement (Item 3), Water Management biosolids contract amendment (Item 4), waterline extension service area fee (Item 5), road salt and aggregates contracts and street sweeper purchases (Items 7-9), the FY 2016-2017 Second Quarter Financial Report (Item 10, pulled), an HR agreement with The Mercer Group (Item 11, pulled), a Police Department 2016 Annual Crime Report presentation scheduled for March 6, proposed stormwater permit modifications (Item 17), FY 2017-2018 budget and FY 2018-2023 CIP public hearings (Items 19-20), and Item 21.

agenda_items.title: Citizens Matters and CeaseFire Durham Policing Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speakers during Citizens Matters addressed community record-clearing efforts and Emerald City's financing of buses to Second Chance Lobby Day in Raleigh. Mark Simmons of CeaseFire Durham presented recommendations to incentivize relationship-based policing, crisis intervention, conflict resolution, engagement with marginalized communities, off-duty training, and related performance evaluation metrics. Staff responded that the Durham Police Department is evaluating PERF's Integrated Communications, Assessment, and Tactics (ICAT) de-escalation and leadership training and noted potential DOJ COPS grant funding.

agenda_items.title: Item 21: Resolution Opposing the Presidential Executive Order on Immigration and Refugee Resettlement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council Member Charlie Reece introduced a resolution opposing the President's January 27, 2017 Executive Order restricting refugee resettlement and travel from seven predominantly Muslim countries, reaffirming Durham as an open and welcoming city, and proclaiming May 6, 2017 as Durham Refugees Day. He cited post-election harassment targeting Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden and a recent bomb threat at a primarily Jewish school in Durham, recognized Clark from World Refugee Durham, and indicated his intent to move to suspend the rules for immediate action. agenda_items.title: Item 17: Proposed Stormwater Permit Modifications and Jordan Lake Ordinance Revisions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council questioned staff and legal counsel Don O'Toole on two alternatives for Jordan Lake basin stormwater rules: revising the permit and ordinances by May 2017 to align with state law, or making no immediate changes until the NPDES permit renewal is submitted in September and issued around February 2018. Don Moffitt confirmed that the federal permit sets a floor allowing stricter state standards if restored, and clarified that keeping existing rules until February 2018 maintains stricter stormwater protections for roughly nine months while exposing the city to developer litigation risk. Staff also reported that a failing detention pond at the Renaissance Center will undergo an Engineering Modification Report remediation from March through October.

agenda_items.title: Item 10 & Item 11: FY 2016-2017 Q2 Financial Report and The Mercer Group HR Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: On Item 10, Council Member Steve Schewel questioned staff on higher-than-projected recycling fees (+42%) and mixed waste transfer fees (+16%), a projected >$7 million positive General Fund variance reducing projected fund balance usage from $15.7 million to $8 million, long-range capital balance planning, and impact fee categories (streets, parks and recreation, and open space). On Item 11, HR staff explained that the Mercer Group engagement is needed to transition away from a one-size-fits-all employee performance evaluation system toward differentiated evaluation models for team-based and specialized roles.

meetings.executive_summary: At the February 9, 2017 City Council Work Session presided over by Mayor Bill Bell (with Steve Schewel excused absent), the Council unanimously approved the City Manager's and City Clerk's priority items (6-0), including referring Item 16 (Durham County Transit Plan update) back to administration and adding five Citizens Matters speakers, and granted an excused absence for Jillian Johnson from the upcoming Saturday Coffee with Council (6-0). During Citizens Matters, speakers from Open for All Durham / Open for All NC advocated for full repeal of House Bill 2 and a local non-discrimination ordinance while recounting prior council concerns over state preemption and legislative retaliation. On Item 14, after receiving only one Joint Venture response to the complex Jackson/Pettigrew Street RFQ, Council voted 6-0 to suspend the rules and advance to Phase 2 evaluation with the Joint Venture (Option 1) ahead of the 2018 tax credit deadline. Council also received an informational presentation on the DCHC MPO Comprehensive Transportation Plan before unanimously setting the Monday night regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the work session to order at 1:03 PM; roll call confirmed Bill Bell, Cora Cole-McFadden, Eddie Davis, Jillian Johnson, Don Moffitt, and Charlie Reece present, while Steve Schewel had an excused absence for his son's wedding. Charlie Reece introduced UNC intern Jake Elliott and Jillian Johnson introduced Duke Heart Leadership intern Priyanka, who was assisting with worker-owned business economic development research. Council unanimously approved the City Manager's priority items (referring Item 16 Durham County Transit Plan update back to administration and adding Citizens Matters items 22-26) and the City Clerk's priority item (Item 21, Museum of Durham History appointment).

agenda_items.title: Draft Regular Agenda Review and Excused Absence Request
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed the upcoming regular agenda, including DPAC Oversight Committee appointments (Items 2-3), street/infrastructure acceptances (Item 4), FY 2016-2017 budget/grant/capital ordinances (Item 5, pulled), Families Moving Forward CDBG case management (Item 6), Brown and Williams Water Treatment Plant upgrades (Item 7), small lift stations rehabilitation (Item 8, pulled), Chapel Hill pool dehumidification (Item 9), Third Fork Creek stream restoration (Item 10, pulled), downtown loop waterline and storm drainage contracts (Items 11-12), utility petition projects (Item 13, pulled), street closings and zoning map changes (Items 17-19), and a Hardwick Drive sidewalk petition (Item 20). Council also approved an excused absence for Jillian Johnson for Saturday's Coffee with Council.

agenda_items.title: Citizens Matters: Open for All NC on House Bill 2 and Non-Discrimination Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A speaker representing Open for All Durham / Open for All NC addressed Council on their newly organized campaign seeking full repeal of House Bill 2 (HB2) and adoption of a citywide non-discrimination ordinance. The speaker noted productive dialogue with individual council members explaining why passing an immediate ordinance would be symbolic under HB2 preemption and politically risky due to potential General Assembly retaliation. The middle portion of the transcript between 00:12:55 and 01:49:13 is omitted in the digest.

agenda_items.title: Item 14: Proposed Jackson/Pettigrew Street Development RFQ Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development staff presented three options after receiving only a single Joint Venture proposal for the challenging L-shaped Jackson/Pettigrew site, which required affordable housing alongside market-rate units, ground-floor commercial space, and structured parking. Option 1 advances to Phase 2 evaluation with the Joint Venture and returns in ~90 days with conceptual drawings, cost estimates, and a draft pre-development agreement ahead of the 2018 tax credit deadline; Option 2 revises the RFQ solely for affordable housing developers; and Option 3 sells the parcel at market rate with proceeds earmarked for affordable housing elsewhere. Council members emphasized leveraging city-owned land for affordable housing, suspended the rules, and voted 6-0 to proceed with Option 1; an unnamed council member departed immediately afterward at 02:13:19 due to a childcare issue.

agenda_items.title: Item 15: Durham-Chapel Hill-Carrboro MPO Comprehensive Transportation Plan
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Transportation Planner Ellen Beckman and DCHC MPO staff Andy Henry presented the draft Comprehensive Transportation Plan (CTP), which replaces the former thoroughfare plan and is referenced in local Unified Development Ordinances (UDOs) to reserve road right-of-way and determine allowable land uses and street classifications. Presenters noted the CTP identifies future transportation improvements without assigning funding priorities, provides downloadable high-resolution PDF poster maps, and remains open for public comment through February 24.

meetings.title: Durham City Council February 6, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: All seven seated members of the Durham City Council met on February 6, 2017, presenting proclamations for Teen Dating Violence Awareness and Prevention Month, Cub Scout Pack 411 Day, and Fred Korematsu Day of Civil Liberties and the Constitution, and swearing in appointees to the Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority and Firefighters' Relief Fund Board of Trustees. Council unanimously approved the remaining consent agenda 7-0 after pulling Item 6, and then unanimously passed Item 6 (Fire and Police compensation and classification plan recommendations) 7-0 following public comment. On Item 8, after extensive public testimony both praising the East Durham Children's Initiative and raising concerns about gentrification, minority business ownership, and formal Community Benefits Agreements, Council unanimously approved 7-0 a $700,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant (requiring an exception to Resolution 9765) for Self-Help Ventures Fund's $10.2 million redevelopment along the Angier-Driver corridor. Council also held the continued public hearing on Item 9 (a proposed charter amendment to eliminate municipal primaries in favor of a general election with runoff), taking no vote while dividing in debate between Eddie Davis (favoring drafting documents for study to save over $100,000 per cycle, with Don Moffitt noting recurring council cost questions while urging no change before 2019) and Bill Bell, Cora Cole-McFadden, Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, and Charlie Reece (opposing eliminating primaries to save money or citing runoff turnout drops, voter-suppression concerns, ranked-choice voting, or true ward/council-size alternatives).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Proclamations, Board Swearing-Ins, and OWASA Water Emergency Thanks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the meeting to order, Cub Scout Pack 411 led the Pledge of Allegiance, and all seven council members answered roll call. Council presented proclamations for Teen Dating Violence Awareness and Prevention Month, Boy Scout and Cub Scout Pack 411 Day, and Fred Korematsu Day (introduced by Charlie Reece and accepted by Dr. Tracy Setauke/Toke of the Japan-America Society of North Carolina), swore in Rodger Lee and Robert D. Teer Jr. to the RDU Airport Authority and Alicia Grant to the Firefighters' Relief Fund Board of Trustees, and heard OWASA Executive Director Ed Kerwin thank Water Management Director Don Greeley and Vicki Westbrook for supplying emergency backup drinking water to Chapel Hill and Carrboro.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Minutes, Appointments, Bid Report, Juniper St. Lease, Solid Waste Annex, South Ellerbe Restoration)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell read the consent agenda titles covering City Council minutes, a Durham City-County Environmental Affairs Board appointment, the December 2016 bid report, a lease with Albright Community Association of Durham at 1017 Juniper Street, a professional services amendment with R&D/RND Architects PA for the Solid Waste Management annex and truck wash project, and a South Ellerbe wetland and stream restoration design contract. Item 6 (Fire and Police compensation) was pulled for public speakers, and the remaining consent items were approved unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Fire and Police Compensation and Classification Plan Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Taken out of order first after the consent vote, Mayor Bell praised staff, police, and fire collaboration on the compensation recommendations and recognized two speakers. Jackie Wagstaff supported raises to help officers afford living in Durham, while Victoria Peterson asked about starting salaries, veteran raises, and promotional exam fairness before Council approved the plan unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Economic Incentive Agreement with Self-Help Ventures Fund ($700,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chris Dickey (Office of Economic and Workforce Development) presented a $700,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant—requiring an exception to Economic Development Policy Resolution 9765—for Self-Help Ventures Fund's $10.2 million commercial renovation of five buildings (~43,000 sq ft) along Angier Avenue and South Driver Street, housing East Durham Children's Initiative, a 100-child daycare accepting subsidies, nonprofit/small-business space, and ~20 public parking spaces. Supporters highlighted EDCI's impact on ~1,300 neighborhood children, while community critics (including James Chavis, Cameron Smith, DeDreana Freeman, Victoria Peterson, and Anita Keith-Foust) warned of displacement, property tax pressure, and limited Black business ownership and urged a formal Community Benefits Agreement (CBA). Council Members Jillian Johnson, Steve Schewel, Cora Cole-McFadden, Charlie Reece, and Mayor Bill Bell backed nonprofit control of the corridor while pressing Self-Help on CBA execution, local hiring, and small-business outreach before approving the grant 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Continued Public Hearing: Proposed City Charter Amendment on Municipal Election Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Attorney Patrick Baker reiterated that the continued public hearing on switching from a primary-and-general municipal election to a single general election with runoff was solely for public comment, with no vote scheduled unless Council later directed staff to return an item. Six speakers opposed eliminating primaries—warning of reduced minority participation, costly citywide runoffs, and incumbency protection—while urging true single-member ward elections and expanding Council from seven to nine seats. In council discussion, Eddie Davis favored advancing documents to study the single-election model to save over $100,000 per cycle, whereas Bill Bell, Cora Cole-McFadden, Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, and Charlie Reece opposed dropping primaries for cost savings and raised turnout, ranked-choice voting, referendum, or true-ward alternatives.

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Items 1-5 and 7, excluding pulled Item 6)
votes.notes: Item 6 considered separately immediately following this vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bell pulled Item 6 for speakers; Council approved the remaining consent items on a single motion.

votes.item_title: Item 6: Fire and Police Compensation and Classification Plan Recommendations
votes.discussion_detail: Following comments from Jackie Wagstaff and Victoria Peterson, Council approved the fire and police compensation and classification recommendations.

votes.item_title: Item 8: Economic Incentive Agreement with Self-Help Ventures Fund ($700,000 Grant)
votes.notes: Required an exception to Economic Development Policy Resolution 9765.
votes.discussion_detail: After extensive public hearing testimony and council questioning of Self-Help representatives Dan Levine and Michael Palmer regarding Community Benefits Agreements, minority business access, and East Durham hiring, Council unanimously approved the $700,000 Neighborhood Revitalization Grant.

disagreements.issue: Proposed Elimination of Municipal Primaries in Favor of General Election with Runoff (Item 9)
disagreements.summary: During the continued public hearing on amending Durham's municipal election process, Council members diverged over whether to pursue eliminating the nonpartisan primary to save election costs or preserve the existing primary-and-general system while exploring alternatives such as instant-runoff voting, voter referenda, or true ward elections.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance administrative documents to study eliminating the municipal primary in favor of a single general election with a majority runoff.
side_a_arguments: Neighboring Raleigh and Chapel Hill use one general election with majority runoffs without voter suppression or disenfranchisement.
Eliminating the primary is estimated to save taxpayers over $100,000 per municipal cycle when primary leaders almost always win the general election.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose eliminating the municipal primary to save money and prioritize voter turnout, voter trust, or alternative reforms (instant-runoff voting, voter referendum, or true ward representation).
side_b_arguments: Bill Bell stated he would never alter election rules to save money; Cora Cole-McFadden described eliminating primaries as voter suppression and urged researching a true ward system and larger council.

Steve Schewel cited Raleigh runoff data (2003 Districts B and D) showing sharp turnout drops in runoffs; Jillian Johnson opposed changing the system now and advocated ranked-choice/instant-runoff voting or a referendum; Charlie Reece supported researching true ward voting and council expansion.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote was taken; Don Moffitt noted that any potential changes should wait until 2019 given 2017 redistricting uncertainty, and the public hearing closed without council direction to return a charter amendment.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting - Legislative Breakfast with Durham Delegation
meetings.executive_summary: On January 27, 2017, Mayor Bill Bell called to order a Special City Council Legislative Breakfast with members of Durham's General Assembly delegation, led in presentation by Senior Assistant to the City Manager Carmisha Wallace alongside City Manager Tom Bonfield. Staff outlined municipal legislative requests including lifting Commercial Driver's License bars for formerly convicted felons needed for Public Works operations, adjusting North Carolina's 618-hour Basic Law Enforcement Training requirement for experienced out-of-state officers, piloting school-zone traffic safety enforcement near schools such as Hillside High School, clarifying authority to use stormwater enterprise funds for flood reduction, empowering City Council to order release of use-of-force body-worn and dashcam footage, and permitting online public hearing notices as an alternative to newspaper print ads. Participants and legislators also discussed annexing unincorporated 'donut hole' pockets, strong judicial and legislative momentum to raise the juvenile justice age to 18, and strategic considerations around repealing House Bill 2 versus passing a local non-discrimination ordinance or resolution. Because this was an informational legislative breakfast, no formal motions or votes were taken.

agenda_items.title: Welcome, Legislative Process Overview, and Tribute to Rep. Paul Luebke
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell opened the legislative breakfast and turned the program over to Senior Assistant to the City Manager Carmisha Wallace, who welcomed City Manager Tom Bonfield, council members, staff, and Durham's General Assembly delegation. Wallace paid tribute to the late Representative Paul Luebke, welcomed his newly appointed successor, and explained how department legislative requests are vetted through the City Manager and Council's legislative subcommittee.

agenda_items.title: General Law Requests: Felon CDL Eligibility, BLET Training Reciprocity, and School Zone Safety Pilot
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented three general law requests: (1) allowing individuals with prior felony convictions who have completed their sentences to obtain Commercial Driver's Licenses (CDLs) for snow plows and heavy equipment, with a legislator noting that federal lifetime bars apply to drug offenses committed using a CMV alongside state disqualifying statutes; (2) adjusting the 618-hour Basic Law Enforcement Training requirement for experienced out-of-state officers such as Durham's new police chief, potentially with NC League of Municipalities backing; and (3) a Transportation Department pilot to curb speeding and improve student safety in school zones such as Alston Avenue near Hillside High School.

agenda_items.title: Stormwater Funds, Police Body-Camera Footage Release, and Electronic Public Hearing Notices
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff requested clarifying statutory language—modeled on Mecklenburg County/Charlotte—to use stormwater enterprise funds for flood reduction, with discussion of seeking an NC Attorney General opinion as interim legal insulation. Staff also sought authority for City Council to order release of body-worn or dashcam video in use-of-force cases, and proposed electronic public hearing notices in lieu of newspaper publication after two Herald-Sun omissions delayed hearings despite $255,000 in annual city ad spending and ~6% household print readership, though a state senator cautioned that residents still rely on centralized newspaper legal notice sections.

agenda_items.title: Donut-Hole Annexation, Raise the Age, and House Bill 2 Strategy
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Discussion covered annexing unincorporated 'donut hole' pockets within city limits to close service-delivery gaps and key advocacy priorities including raising the juvenile justice age to 18, which a legislator noted had gained backing from the NC Supreme Court Chief Justice and Administrative Office of the Courts. On House Bill 2 (HB2), legislators and city participants discussed whether enacting a local non-discrimination ordinance now could invite General Assembly retaliation while repeal compromise talks were underway, and noted that passing a non-binding resolution (as Charlotte did) remained an alternative.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the January 19, 2017 City Council Work Session presided over by Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden (with Mayor Bill Bell absent), the Council unanimously approved an excused absence for Steve Schewel for the February 9 work session due to his son's wedding. Council reviewed draft agenda items including a proposed five-year lease at 1017 Juniper Street—where a county grant required a 10-year term—a Solid Waste truck wash design amendment, a proposed City Charter amendment for municipal elections, and a Wildlands Engineering item. On the priority Item 6, HR, Budget, Fire, and Police staff presented updated peer-market compensation analyses and recommended Alternative 1 (100% of market without geographic adjustment) at a six-month implementation cost of $1.8 million from the $2.5 million already budgeted, while resident Shirley Ellis urged Council to fund full DPD pay and staffing increases from the IACP study. Council also noted six votes for an appointee to the City-County Environmental Affairs Board, unanimously set the Monday regular meeting agenda, and voted to enter closed session on a motion by Don Moffitt.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Excused Absence for Steve Schewel, and Priority Item
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden called the January 19, 2017 work session to order at 1:00 PM and directed the clerk to call the roll. Council Member Steve Schewel requested and received an excused absence by unanimous voice vote for the February 9 work session to attend his son's wedding in Louisiana. The City Manager identified Item 6 (Fire and Police compensation and classification plan recommendations) as the administration's priority item.

agenda_items.title: Draft Agenda Review and Proposed 1017 Juniper Street Lease
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed upcoming agenda items including a proposed community association lease for city-owned property at 1017 Juniper Street, Item 5 (R&D Architects PA amendment for the Solid Waste Management annex and truck wash project), Item 6 (public safety compensation), Item 7 (Public Works), and a proposed City Charter amendment regarding Durham municipal election procedures. Discussion on the 1017 Juniper Street lease highlighted a mismatch between a county grant's 10-year lease requirement and the city's five-year lease containing termination clauses such as potential trail construction.

agenda_items.title: Item 6: Fire and Police Compensation and Classification Plan Recommendations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: HR, Budget Management Services, Fire, and Police staff presented new pay structures and peer-survey comparisons (geographically adjusted, unadjusted, and 98% of market) for police and fire recruits, officers, and firefighters, recommending Alternative 1 (100% of market without geographic adjustment) at $1.8 million for six-month implementation within the $2.5 million already allocated. Council members praised Fire Department first-responder medical response and DPD emergency chaplains; resident Shirley Ellis urged Council to implement full DPD pay and staffing increases recommended by the $91,000 IACP study, pointing to the city's $54 million reserve balance. Don Moffitt confirmed the $1.8 million six-month implementation figure.

agenda_items.title: Item 7 (Wildlands Engineering), Board Appointment Preview, Agenda Setting, and Closed Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council took up Item 7 with Wildlands Engineering (pulled by Don Moffitt) and noted six votes supporting an appointee (Jessica) for an at-large seat on the City-County Environmental Affairs Board. Council then approved the Monday night regular agenda (Consent items 1-7 and Public Hearings items 8-9) by unanimous voice vote and passed Don Moffitt's motion to enter closed session with transportation staff and two outside parties.

meetings.title: Durham City Council January 17, 2017
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Bill Bell absent on an excused absence, Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden presided over the six-member Durham City Council on January 17, 2017, approving the consent agenda (Items 2-11) 6-0. On the public hearing agenda, Council unanimously approved 6-0 the zoning map change and consistency statement for 108 Celeste Circle (Item 12, Central Dermatology parking lot), unanimously designated the J.A. Whitted School building and 4.1 acres as a local historic landmark 6-0 (Item 14), and voted 6-0 to receive public comments on the FY 2017-18 Annual Action Plan (Item 15) after hearing urgent pleas from home-repair nonprofits and Durham Community Land Trustees. Council split 5-1 on Item 13 (street closing of Nevada Avenue, Chester Springs Road, and Hickman Avenue), voting to delay consideration until February 20, 2017 so the developer and Tuscaloosa-Lakewood neighbors could meet (Ayes: Cora Cole-McFadden, Steve Schewel, Jillian Johnson, Charlie Reece, Eddie Davis; Nay: Don Moffitt). Finally, on Supplemental Item 17 (proposed charter amendment on municipal elections), Council heard four speakers opposing elimination of the primary and voted 6-0 to continue the public hearing to February 6, 2017.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Neighborhood Spotlight Award, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden opened the meeting, noting Mayor Bill Bell's excused absence, and Council Member Eddie Davis led the Pledge of Allegiance. Cole-McFadden presented the January 2017 Neighborhood Spotlight Award to James Clark of Autumn Woods/Woodcroft, Steve Schewel promoted the new DHIC-administered NeighborhoodLift $7,500 down-payment assistance program, and Don Moffitt recognized a community forum organized by Robin Cooper addressing violent crime solutions.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Trustees Appointment, HOME Loan Pool, NC-98 Study, Water/Sewer, Paving, and IT Security)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield, City Attorney Patrick Baker, and the City Clerk reported no priority items. Mayor Pro Tempore Cole-McFadden read Consent Items 2 through 11 covering the Firefighters' Relief Fund Board appointment, a HOME community partners loan pool with NCHFA, the NC-98 corridor study with NCDOT and Raleigh, Central Park waterline and sanitary sewer/WRF contracts, security improvements, an NC-751 sewer extension, Ravenstone and Stonehill Estates paving, and a managed network security contract.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — 108 Celeste Circle (Case Z160006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Kyle Taylor presented Case Z160006 to rezone 0.46 acres from RS-20 to Planned Office and Institutional with a Development Plan (OI(D)) for a Central Dermatology surface parking lot with 100-year stormwater control, added evergreen screening, a security gate, and no driveway access onto Celeste Circle. Applicant representative Dan Jewell noted Eastwood Lake Neighborhood Association concerns were resolved, and Council Member Steve Schewel—who opposed an earlier UNC proposal—moved approval.

agenda_items.title: Street Closing of Portions of Nevada Avenue, Chester Springs Road, and Hickman Avenue
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Kyle Taylor presented a request to close 1,505 linear feet of unopened paper-street right-of-way along jurisdictional streams where B. Wallace Design & Construction planned a 14-lot by-right single-family subdivision. Five neighbors requested a delay citing limited notice, stormwater/stream impacts, neighborhood character, and lack of public park space, while applicant Jared Eadens emphasized the closure avoids stream crossings and Don Moffitt probed connectivity and existing 27-lot platting. Steve Schewel moved to delay consideration until February 20, 2017 for neighbor-developer dialogue, passing 5-1 with Moffitt opposed.

agenda_items.title: J.A. Whitted School Local Historic Landmark Designation (Case LD160001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Karla Rosenberg presented Case LD160001 (Belk Architecture) to designate both the historic J.A. Whitted School structure and 4.1 acres at 200 East Umstead Street as a local landmark, which the Historic Preservation Commission recommended 3-2 over two votes for building-only designation. Architect Andy Scholl explained preserving open lawns protects mid-century sightlines, developer Darrell Jones estimated ~$20 million in total post-renovation value (prompting Steve Schewel to note higher eventual tax revenue and tax-break impact than the 2016 $1.5M valuation), and Council unanimously approved the designation.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: FY 2017-18 Annual Action Plan (CDBG, HOME, ESG, and HOPWA Needs)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers opened the first of two annual public hearings on projected FY 2017-18 HUD entitlements (~$1.8M CDBG, ~$800k HOME, ~$160k ESG, ~$290k HOPWA). Ten speakers—including Durham Community Land Trustees (seeking HOME funds for 54 newly acquired East Durham rental units), Rebuilding Together, Senior PharmAssist, Wilma Dillard, Resources for Seniors, Preservation Durham, Habitat for Humanity, and Braggtown/East End residents—urged increased home-repair funding, coordinated intake, and rental preservation. Don Moffitt highlighted county tax-abatement options and maintaining existing affordable stock, and Steve Schewel requested funding estimates from the repair collaborative and follow-up on a Braggtown playground before Council voted 6-0 to receive comments.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: Proposed City Charter Amendment on Municipal Election Process
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Attorney Patrick Baker distributed an FAQ memo explaining that Council was only receiving comments on changing municipal elections from a primary-and-general format to a single general election with runoff, and no action would occur without future affirmative council direction. Four speakers—Anita Keith-Foust, Jackie Wagstaff, Chris Tiffany, and Jim Vara—opposed eliminating primaries and urged exploring instant-runoff voting or true ward elections. Council Member Jillian Johnson advocated ranked-choice voting, noted potential 2017 cost-sharing with court-ordered state elections, and requested continuing the hearing so residents at an overlapping community meeting could speak on February 6, 2017.

votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Moved by Council Member Steve Schewel after noting substantial improvements over the earlier proposal two years prior; approved rezoning from RS-20 to OI(D).

votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell absent.

votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Formally received public hearing testimony on CDBG, HOME, ESG, and HOPWA funding priorities.

votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell absent.
votes.discussion_detail: Continued the municipal election charter amendment public hearing to the February 6, 2017 meeting at Council Member Jillian Johnson's request so residents attending another meeting could be heard.

disagreements.issue: Delay of Street Closing for Nevada Avenue, Chester Springs Road, and Hickman Avenue (Item 13)
disagreements.summary: Council voted 5-1 to delay the proposed closure of 1,505 linear feet of unopened paper streets for a 14-lot by-right subdivision until February 20, 2017, with Don Moffitt dissenting.
disagreements.side_a_position: Delay consideration for one month until February 20, 2017 so the developer and Tuscaloosa-Lakewood residents can meet.
side_a_arguments: Although the 14-lot subdivision is by-right and met statutory notice rules for immediate abutters, surrounding neighbors felt blindsided and wanted time to discuss stream, stormwater, and open-space concerns.
Steve Schewel noted he anticipated supporting the street closure after a 30-day window for neighbor-developer communication.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose delaying the street closing decision.
side_b_arguments: Don Moffitt questioned whether closing the right-of-way sacrificed street connectivity and a potential connection from Chester Springs Road to Ward Street.
Moffitt also confirmed with planning staff that 27 lots were already platted by right compared to 14 proposed homes, and opposed the delay motion.
disagreements.resolution: Motion to delay consideration until February 20, 2017 passed 5-1 at 00:56:03 with Don Moffitt voting No.

meetings.title: City Council Work Session
meetings.executive_summary: At the January 5, 2017 City Council Work Session, Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden opened the meeting, led a moment of silence commemorating community leader Sharon Elliott Bynum and recently deceased civic figures, and read Mayor Bill Bell's National Mentoring Month proclamation honoring Dewarren Langley. Council approved by voice vote the City Manager's priority item—adding supplemental Item 16, a proposal for a city forgivable loan program—and the City Clerk's priority items referring Item 1 minutes back to the Clerk's office and adding the proclamation. Council reviewed upcoming agenda items including a recreation center fee-waiver update request ahead of the budget cycle, an NC Housing Finance Agency HOME loan pool, an NC 98 corridor study, Central Park waterline work achieving 40% MUBE participation, and remaining street and stormwater remediation for failed 2010-2011 subdivisions. During extensive discussion of Item 16 with Mayor Bell participating, Council members including Steve Schewel expressed support for the spirit of using forgivable loans to assist longtime homeowners facing property tax burdens while asking staff to examine tax-abatement benchmarks from cities such as Philadelphia ahead of a January 10 joint committee review, before unanimously setting the regular meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Moment of Silence, Priority Items, and National Mentoring Month Proclamation
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden called the January 5, 2017 work session to order, conducted roll call, and led a moment of silence for Sharon Elliott Bynum and other recently deceased community members while an unnamed council member noted leaving before 2:00 PM for George Lawrence's memorial service. Council approved the City Manager's priority item adding supplemental Item 16 (proposal for a city forgivable loan program) and the City Clerk's priority items referring Item 1 minutes back to the Clerk and adding a proclamation. Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden then read Mayor Bill Bell's proclamation recognizing National Mentoring Month and honoring Dewarren Langley.

agenda_items.title: Recreation Center Fee Trial Request and Draft Regular Agenda Review
agenda_items.discussion_summary: A council member requested a pre-budget update on the trial waiver of recreation center fees, citing Denver's policy making recreation centers free for youth 18 and under. Staff and Council reviewed upcoming agenda items including adding two firefighters to the Relief Fund Board of Trustees, Item 3 (HOME loan pool agreement with the NC Housing Finance Agency), Item 4 (interlocal agreement with NCDOT and Raleigh for the NC 98 Corridor Study), Item 5 (Central Park water line replacement amendment, with praise for 40% MUBE contractor participation), Item 13 (Nevada Avenue, Chester Springs Road, and Hickman Avenue street closings), and Item 14 (historic school landmark designation).

agenda_items.title: Engineering Workforce Recruitment, Failed Subdivisions Remediation, and Editorial Note
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Presenters discussed specialized water and wastewater engineering recruitment challenges and outreach at university career fairs such as UNC Charlotte. Public Works Assistant Director Tasha Johnson responded to council questions on remaining failed/struggling subdivisions from 2010-2011, detailing micro-surfacing street work and confirming that stormwater facility assessments for two failed subdivisions will return in a later phase. Council also flagged a spelling correction for Shirley Caesar's name in agenda materials.

agenda_items.title: Item 16: Proposal for a City Forgivable Loan Program for Property Tax Relief
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council examined Mayor Bill Bell's memo proposing a city forgivable loan program to help homeowners facing rising property tax bills and potential delinquency publication. Council questioned Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and City Manager Tom Bonfield on whether other cities—specifically Philadelphia—use tax abatement programs; Steve Schewel and another council member praised the proposal's intent while questioning the most efficient delivery mechanism.
